briefs.legalName: Erasure After a Nolle, and Motion to Nolle a Continued Charge, C.G.S. § 54-142a(c)
briefs.publicName: Records erased after a case was nolled
briefs.mechanism: Where a charge has been nolled, records shall be erased once thirteen months have elapsed since the nolle. Separately, where a charge was continued at the prosecutor's request and thirteen months have passed with no prosecution or other disposition, the charge shall be nolled on motion of the arrested person, and erasure then follows the nolle rules. The second is an affirmative motion the participant can make; it is the one part of this track that is not passive.

briefs.legalName: Expungement of a Deferred Judgment Record on Discharge from Probation
briefs.publicName: Clearing a deferred judgment after probation
briefs.mechanism: On discharge from probation where judgment was deferred under § 907.3, the court's criminal record with reference to the deferred judgment shall be expunged, together with dismissed counts in the same charging instrument and other related dismissed charges arising from the same transaction or occurrence or a common scheme or plan. The record is not expunged until financial obligations in that case are paid. The deferred judgment itself remains on the state court administrator's deferred judgment docket and is not expunged. This mechanism sits outside Rules 2.80 through 2.86 and has no Rule 2.86 form.

briefs.publicName: Expunging a conviction after a pardon that authorizes expungement
briefs.mechanism: Where the Governor has issued a pardon that specifically authorizes expungement, a verified petition may be filed with the Chief Judge of the circuit of conviction, a judge of that circuit designated by the Chief Judge, or in counties under 3,000,000 inhabitants the presiding trial judge. briefs.publicName: Filing early as a problem-solving court or diversion graduate
briefs.mechanism: Added by the Clean Slate Act effective June 1, 2026. The triggering event is fulfilment of the diversion terms, and nothing else.

briefs.legalName: Petition for Expungement of a Kansas Arrest Record under K.S.A. 22-2410
briefs.publicName: Expunging an arrest that did not lead to a conviction
briefs.mechanism: Any person who has been arrested in Kansas may petition the district court to expunge the arrest record. There is no waiting period. On filing, the court sets a hearing date and causes notice to be given to the prosecuting attorney and the arresting law enforcement agency, and the official court file is separated from other court records and disclosed only to a judge, designated court staff, the prosecuting attorney, the arresting agency or others by court order. At the hearing the court shall order the arrest record and subsequent court proceedings expunged on finding that the arrest occurred because of mistaken identity, that a court found there was no probable cause for the arrest, that the petitioner was found not guilty, or that expungement would be in the best interests of justice and charges have been dismissed or no charges have been or are likely to be filed. This is the correct route for an arrest-only record: K.S.A. 21-6614 expunges a conviction or a diversion and related arrest records, so with neither there is nothing for it to attach to.

destination.name: Clerk of the district court

briefs.legalName: Segregation of Arrest Records After Acquittal, Dismissal or Withdrawal of Charges (KRS 17.142)
briefs.publicName: Ask agencies to file away the record of an arrest that went nowhere
briefs.mechanism: A law enforcement or other public agency holding arrest records, fingerprints, photographs or other data must, on the written request of the arrestee, segregate those records into a file separate from those of convicted persons where the person was found innocent or all charges relating to the offence were dismissed or withdrawn. The person may instead apply to the court, which shall forthwith issue an order to all law enforcement agencies. Each agency must notify every agency it shared the records with, and the segregated record must show the disposition. Records subject to KRS 431.076 or KRS 431.078 are sealed under those statutes instead.
briefs.venue: For the court application, the court in which the case was tried, or in which it would have been tried had charges been filed. For the written requests, no venue: they go to the agencies.

destination.name: The trial court on the application route, and each record-holding agency on the written-request route
destination.detail: The court application is filed with the circuit court clerk in the county of the case and produces an order binding all law enforcement agencies. The written requests are posted by the participant to each agency they identify. The two routes are independent: either obtains segregation, and a participant may use both.

briefs.legalName: Motion to Set Aside Conviction and Dismiss Prosecution; Rule to Show Cause; Order of Dismissal (La. C.Cr.P. art. 987)
briefs.publicName: Set aside a conviction and dismiss the prosecution after a deferred sentence
briefs.mechanism: Article 987 supplies the forms to be used for a motion to set aside a conviction and dismiss the prosecution, the rule to show cause, and the order of dismissal. It is not an expungement. It is the predicate filing that converts a completed deferred sentence into a set-aside conviction and a dismissed prosecution under Article 894(B) for a misdemeanour or Article 893(E) for a felony, which in turn unlocks Article 977(A)(1) or Article 978(A)(1). As pleaded on the statutory form, eligibility is that the period of the deferred sentence has run and the petitioner has successfully completed the terms of probation. The instrument is in three parts: the Motion; a Rule to Show Cause ordering the district attorney to show cause why the motion should not be granted; and the Order of Dismissal. The motion's own prayer asks for relief after a contradictory hearing with the district attorney's office. Service is on the district attorney and on the attorney for the defendant or the defendant. The form carries parallel signature blocks for counsel and for an unrepresented mover, so it is drafted for pro se use. Source note Acts 2014, No. 145.

briefs.publicName: Correcting a record created by identity theft
briefs.mechanism: The review recorded the statutory basis and scope of CR300 as not established and made it the track's build blocker. It is now established, from the official form's own face and from the statute it cites. CR300 states: Pursuant to sections 575.120.4 and 610.123, RSMo, I hereby request that the court issue an order to expunge the following arrest and court records that falsely identify me and to correct the arrest and court records to accurately reflect the identity of the defendant. Its footer carries the same two citations. § 575.120 is the false impersonation offense, and subsection 4 supplies the victim's civil remedy: any person who is the victim of a false impersonation and whose identity has been falsely reported in arrest or conviction records may move for expungement and correction of those records under the procedures set forth in § 610.123, and upon a showing that a substantial number of identifying factors of the victim was falsely ascribed to the person actually arrested or convicted, the court shall order the false identifying factors contained in the arrest and court records amended to correctly and accurately identify the defendant and shall expunge the incorrect and inaccurate factors from the arrest and court records. That single provision answers every question the review left open. The relief is correction plus targeted expungement of the false identifying factors, not expungement of the case. The proof is a substantial number of identifying factors falsely ascribed, which is a different and in some ways lower showing than § 610.145's identity-used-without-permission finding. Relief is mandatory on that showing: the court shall order. The procedure is § 610.123's, which means a verified petition in the civil division of the circuit court in the county of the arrest, the eleven mandatory contents whose absence requires dismissal, the standard fingerprint card filed with the petition and forwarded to the central repository, defendants named with the order reaching only those named, and a hearing set no sooner than thirty days from filing with reasonable notice to each named entity. And critically the section reaches arrest or conviction records: unlike § 610.145 it does not require that the charge against the participant was dismissed or that they were acquitted, because the point is that somebody else was arrested or convicted under the participant's identity. The adopted Batch 2 memorandum's direction to keep this route separate from CR301 is therefore not merely preserved but strengthened: they are different statutes, different courts, different divisions, different proof and different remedies. The memorandum's primary-authority line cites § 610.145 for both forms; the form's own citation controls and is recorded as a correction.
briefs.venue: The civil division of the circuit court in the county of the arrest (§ 610.123.1, incorporated by § 575.120.4), which CR300 states on its face: I am filing this petition in the county where the arrest occurred. The court sets the hearing no sooner than thirty days from filing under § 610.123.3.

briefs.legalName: Petition to Expunge Records Related to an Arrest for an Eligible Crime (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 610.140.7)
briefs.publicName: An arrest that never became a charge
briefs.mechanism: Section 610.140.7 is a distinct petition inside the general expungement section and it was read verbatim from the Revisor's current text. It provides that a petition to expunge records related to an arrest for an eligible crime may be made in accordance with the provisions of the section to a court of competent jurisdiction in the county where the petitioner was arrested no earlier than eighteen months from the date of arrest, provided that during that time the petitioner has not been charged and has not been found guilty of any misdemeanor or felony offense. Two things follow and both were disputed in the retained review. The waiting period is eighteen months, not three years: the internal LegalEase reference was correct and the secondary source quoting three years was quoting a superseded version. And venue is the county of arrest, which differs from the court-of-charge rule that governs the conviction route. The eleven exclusion categories in § 610.140.3 apply unchanged, because the arrest must be for an eligible crime. Relief is mandatory under § 610.140.8 once the criteria are met, the clerk's notice, the thirty-day objection window, the sixty-day hearing rule and the six-month decision deadline all apply, and the effect is closure under § 610.120. This route is not § 610.122: that is a narrower false-information or qualifying-moving-violation mechanism with a different court, a different division, a fingerprint card, notarization and destruction rather than closure.
briefs.venue: A court of competent jurisdiction in the county where the petitioner was arrested (§ 610.140.7). This is the arrest county, and it is deliberately different from the conviction route's court-of-charge rule. Where the participant was arrested in one county and any charge would have been filed in another, the arrest county controls this petition.

briefs.legalName: Petition for Expungement or Resentencing of a Marijuana Conviction While Currently Serving (Mont. Code Ann. § 16-12-113(1)-(4), (8)-(12))
briefs.publicName: Marijuana conviction expungement or resentencing while serving a sentence
briefs.mechanism: Under § 16-12-113(1) a person CURRENTLY SERVING a sentence for an act that is permitted under Title 16, chapter 12, or that is punishable by a lesser sentence under that chapter than the person was awarded, may petition for expungement or resentencing. Section 16-12-113(2) directs the court to presume the petitioner satisfies the criteria unless the county attorney provides a reasonable basis otherwise, and, where the criteria are satisfied, to grant the petition UNLESS the court determines that granting it would pose an unreasonable risk of danger to public safety. That public-safety override does not appear in the subsection (6) pathway used by the completed-sentence track, and it is the principal reason the two are separate mechanisms rather than branches. Section 16-12-113(3) requires credit for time already served and prohibits supervision after resentencing; § 16-12-113(4) prohibits a term longer than the original sentence and prohibits reinstatement of charges dismissed under a negotiated plea agreement. Sections 16-12-114 through 16-12-116 define an expungement or resentencing of marijuana conviction court and authorise appointment of a decriminalized marijuana conviction expungement judge with the authority and power of an elected district court judge. Procedure is governed by the AF 22-0129 Temporary Rules and the Office of the Court Administrator publishes Form A specifically for the currently-serving posture, with the same Certificate of Service and Proposed Order.
briefs.venue: Whichever court sentenced the participant, on the same three caption options as the completed-sentence track. Sections 16-12-114 and 16-12-115 additionally define an expungement or resentencing of marijuana conviction court and permit appointment of a designated decriminalized marijuana conviction expungement judge; whether any such judge has been appointed, and whether that changes the practical filing destination in any county, is unresolved.

Montana's three words are not interchangeable and participant copy must keep them apart. Expungement under § 46-18-1103(1) means to permanently destroy, delete or erase a record from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law-enforcement agencies and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Removal is the DOJ term for deleting a non-conviction record. Redesignation and resentencing are MMRTA outcomes and are neither.

The Misdemeanor Expungement in Montana packet (ER-100, ER-200 and the Statement of Inability to Pay Court Costs and Fees) and the Dismissal After Completing a Deferred Sentence packet (DS-100 and DS-200) are stamped '© 2025 Montana Legal Services Association and Montana Supreme Court Access to Justice Commission. This form may be used for non-commercial purposes only.' Expungement.ai is a paid product, so reproducing or distributing them inside a packet is a commercial use. They are drafting references only: never generated, never relabelled, never converted, never lightly rewritten, never runtime-selectable and never generation_allowed. The restriction changes source use, not the existence of the mechanism.

The court order is not the end in Montana. Under § 46-18-1110(2)(b) the person whose records are being expunged, not the court and not the clerk, must send the order to the arresting agency, the prosecutor, the clerk and the Department of Justice, together with fingerprints and the DOJ form; § 46-18-204(2) holds the same pattern for deferred dismissals; and the OCA MMRTA instructions say the same. A Montana packet that stops at a signed court order leaves the conviction sitting on the participant's background check.

No participant-facing statement that the participant may deny the conviction after expungement, after a deferred dismissal, or after a non-conviction removal. No Montana perjury shield or restoration-to-prior-status provision was located in any of the three statutes, and whether a cleared record may lawfully be denied is a hard self-help stop.

LegalEase does not choose among expungement, redesignation as a misdemeanour, and redesignation as a civil infraction. These are materially different outcomes with different consequences, the form requires the participant to choose, and the election is the participant's alone. Any analysis of which outcome is better is legal advice and triggers handoff.

The offence-mapping question is a self-help boundary: whether the historical conduct is now permitted, or is now punishable by a lesser sentence, under Title 16, chapter 12 requires mapping decades-old charging language and quantities against the current chapter, and it is the central legal question of the track. LegalEase presents the enumerated statutory list and the participant selects; the free-text specify-offence path is an attorney handoff.

One complete form set per conviction, never a consolidated petition. The OCA instructions require a separate form for each conviction even where the convictions occurred at the same time. This is the opposite of the misdemeanour expungement track, where one petition covers the whole record, and the rules engine must not generalise across the two.

The OCA instructions state expressly that the participant must follow all applicable filing rules including local filing rules, and route the participant to the Court Locator for local rules and contact information. This is an acknowledged local-practice dependency and is built as a required lookup step.

briefs.legalName: Petition and Order of Expunction of Nonviolent Misdemeanor Convictions under G.S. 15A-145.5
briefs.publicName: Expunge a nonviolent North Carolina misdemeanor conviction
briefs.mechanism: On petition, the court may expunge nonviolent misdemeanor convictions. Nonviolent is defined by exclusion in G.S. 15A-145.5(a). The waiting period is three years for one nonviolent misdemeanor conviction, for petitions filed on or after July 9, 2025, and seven years for more than one, each measured from the conviction and completion of any active, probationary or post-release sentence, whichever is later. The petitioner consents to two record checks: the AOC checks for prior expunctions and the DPS State Bureau of Investigation checks for prior convictions. The district attorney is given notice and may be heard.
briefs.venue: Superior Court of the county where the charge was brought.

destination.name: Clerk of superior court, county where the charge was brought
destination.detail: Statewide statute with county venue. After the petition is filed the AOC checks for prior expunctions, the DPS State Bureau of Investigation checks for prior convictions, and the district attorney is given notice and may be heard. On a grant the order directs the SBI, DPS, DMV, the AOC, the clerk and the arresting agency to expunge the records, and the clerk notifies State and local agencies under G.S. 15A-150.

briefs.legalName: Petition and Order of Expunction of Dismissed Charges under G.S. 15A-146(a) and (a1)
briefs.publicName: Clear a North Carolina charge that was dismissed
briefs.mechanism: On petition, the court expunges the records of a charge dismissed by the State or by the court, for a single dismissal under subsection (a) and for multiple dismissals under subsection (a1). There is no prior-conviction bar and no prior-expunction bar; the 2017 legislation eliminated the prior-expunction bar. A judge may grant the petition without a hearing under subsection (a6). Any petition under this section must be on a form approved by the Administrative Office of the Courts.
briefs.venue: Superior Court of the county where the charge was brought.

destination.name: Clerk of superior court, county where the charge was brought
destination.detail: Statewide statute with county venue. The petition is filed with the clerk of superior court on the AOC-approved form. Excluding automatic expunctions under subsection (a4), the clerk notifies State and local agencies of the order as provided in G.S. 15A-150 and forwards a certified copy to the Division of Motor Vehicles for expunction of any civil revocation where the underlying criminal charge is also expunged.

briefs.legalName: Routing of DNA Profile Removal (N.D.C.C. § 31-13-07)
briefs.publicName: Where to go about a North Dakota DNA profile
briefs.mechanism: An individual whose DNA profile is in the state database may petition the district court to seal the court record on enumerated grounds. On receipt of a certified order the laboratory expunges all identifiable information and destroys all samples, and the sealed record may not be opened even by order of the court. A detention, arrest or conviction based on database information is not invalidated even if the samples should have been expunged.
briefs.venue: North Dakota district court, with the certified order then delivered to the State Crime Laboratory.

destination.name: No destination. This node routes rather than files
destination.detail: The node routes to counsel, which the controlling review makes an express handoff trigger for DNA matters. A participant-facing petition does exist under N.D.C.C. § 31-13-07(1) and no official form is published, so the route is legally capable of being built as a custom pleading.

briefs.legalName: Petition of Eligibility for Annulment of a Violation or Class B Misdemeanor Conviction, Streamlined Mandatory Route (RSA 651:5, III(a)(2) and III(b)(2))
briefs.publicName: The fast New Hampshire annulment route for a recent minor conviction
briefs.mechanism: For a violation or a class B misdemeanor with a conviction date on or after January 1, 2019 where that offence was the highest offense of conviction, the court submits a notice of its determination to the person and to the prosecutor. The prosecutor has twenty days from receipt to object, and only on two grounds: that the offence is not eligible for annulment, or that the person has not completed all the terms and conditions of the sentence. If no timely objection is made, or the objection is denied, the court shall annul the conviction. This is the only conviction route in New Hampshire where the paragraph I rehabilitation and public welfare discretion does not decide the outcome, and the only one with a defined objection clock and defined objection grounds. Paragraphs V, VI, VII and VIII still apply. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
briefs.venue: The court that disposed of the charge. One petition per charge.

destination.name: Clerk of the disposing court
destination.detail: The court reviews the petition, determines eligibility, and submits a notice of its determination to the person and to the prosecutor. The prosecutor's twenty-day objection window runs from receipt of that notice. The Judicial Branch checklist notes that for a violation or class B misdemeanor conviction after January 1, 2019 the court reviews the request and may issue an order conditionally granting the petition, with notice to follow.

briefs.legalName: Petition to Annul the Record of a Non-Conviction Disposed of Before January 1, 2019 (RSA 651:5, II)
briefs.publicName: Annul an older New Hampshire arrest that did not end in a conviction
briefs.mechanism: A person found not guilty, or whose case was dismissed or not prosecuted, may petition at any time for annulment of the arrest record, the court record, or both, where the offence was disposed of before January 1, 2019 or otherwise falls outside the automatic route in paragraph II-a. Relief is discretionary under paragraph I: the court may annul if in its opinion the annulment will assist rehabilitation and be consistent with the public welfare, and it may grant or deny without a hearing unless the petitioner requests one. The court provides a copy of the petition to the prosecutor, who may be heard on the interest of justice, and the Department of Corrections performs a statutory investigation. RSA 651:5, IX and X(d) exempt a person found not guilty or whose case was dismissed or not prosecuted from the $100 Department of Corrections investigation fee and the $100 Department of Safety and state police fees. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
briefs.venue: The Circuit Court District Division or Superior Court that disposed of the charge. The Judicial Branch checklist directs that each petition be filed with the court where the charge was disposed.

destination.name: Clerk of the disposing court
destination.detail: New Hampshire is a unified statewide court system with no local variation identified, so the only venue question is which court disposed of the charge. One petition per charge; petitions filed at the same time in one court location share a single $125.00 filing fee.

briefs.publicName: Annul the record of a New Hampshire conviction that was vacated
briefs.mechanism: A person convicted of a criminal offence whose conviction was subsequently vacated by a court may petition for annulment where the offence falls outside the automatic route in paragraph II-a. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.

briefs.legalName: Automated "Clean Slate" Process (N.J.S.A. 2C:52-5.4)
briefs.publicName: New Jersey's automatic record clearing, and where it stands
briefs.mechanism: The State shall develop and implement an automated process by which all convictions and related records are rendered inaccessible to the public, through sealing, expungement or an equivalent process, for a person convicted of one or more crimes or offences, unless the person has a conviction not subject to expungement under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2(b) or (c), upon the expiration of ten years. A task force was established to design it and reported in 2022. The process is not operational: Assembly Bill A5095, introduced May 14, 2026, states that it still does not exist and that eligible people must still file a petition with the court. The section also requires that a person's convictions and criminal history be restored in certain circumstances if the person is subsequently convicted of a crime not subject to expungement. Expungement in New Jersey is defined at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-1 as the extraction and isolation of criminal justice records, not their destruction. In most contexts the person may then answer that the event did not occur. Certain law enforcement, judicial and specified licensing uses survive under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-27. The relief reaches New Jersey records only: federal and out-of-state records are untouched, although out-of-state convictions still count when assessing eligibility. There is no federal immigration effect.
briefs.venue: No venue. The process, when built, runs on the State's records rather than on a filing.

destination.name: The State of New Jersey, once the automated process is established
destination.detail: Nothing is filed and nothing is generated. The participant is told the true status: the automation does not exist yet, the petition route is open, and the petition route is what they should use. The New Jersey State Police expungement status portal is the place to check a record's status.

briefs.legalName: Expungement of an Indictable Conviction (N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2)
briefs.publicName: Expunge a New Jersey felony conviction
briefs.mechanism: "Indictable offence" is New Jersey's word for a felony and is heard in Superior Court; "disorderly persons" and "petty disorderly persons" offences are the misdemeanour equivalents and are usually Municipal Court matters. An expungement application may be presented where the person has one crime conviction and no subsequent crime conviction; or one crime and no more than three disorderly persons or petty disorderly persons offences; or multiple convictions all listed in a single judgment of conviction; or multiple convictions that were interdependent or closely related in circumstances and committed as part of a sequence of events within a comparatively short period, regardless of the individual conviction or sentencing dates. The single-judgment and closely-related routes carry no numeric cap, which is the difference between a five-year petition and a ten-year Clean Slate petition for a participant with several convictions from one episode. The ordinary waiting period is five years from the latest of the most recent conviction, payment of any court-ordered financial assessment, satisfactory completion of probation or parole, or release from incarceration. Expungement in New Jersey is defined at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-1 as the extraction and isolation of criminal justice records, not their destruction. In most contexts the person may then answer that the event did not occur. Certain law enforcement, judicial and specified licensing uses survive under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-27. The relief reaches New Jersey records only: federal and out-of-state records are untouched, although out-of-state convictions still count when assessing eligibility. There is no federal immigration effect.
briefs.venue: The Superior Court in the county in which the person resides, or a county in which one or more of the person's convictions were adjudged. This is a real choice and is surfaced to the participant. The venue language was read in the official bill text of A5826, which amends N.J.S.2C:52-2 by striking "most recent conviction for a crime was" and inserting the residence-or-conviction-county rule; the 2019 enacted text of P.L.2019, c.269 carried the earlier formulation.

briefs.publicName: Expunge a New Jersey municipal ordinance violation
briefs.mechanism: A conviction for a municipal ordinance offence may be expunged after two years, which New Jersey Courts confirms on its official self-help page. The petition, the statements, the order for hearing and the proposed order are the same Judiciary kit documents as the other tracks, filed in the Superior Court with no filing fee. The full text of N.J.S.A. 2C:52-4 was not read at an official channel, and whether ordinance convictions count toward the offence caps on the other tracks is recorded as an open question. Expungement in New Jersey is defined at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-1 as the extraction and isolation of criminal justice records, not their destruction. In most contexts the person may then answer that the event did not occur. Certain law enforcement, judicial and specified licensing uses survive under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-27. briefs.legalName: Petition to Expunge Arrest Records and Public Records upon Identity Theft (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-3)
briefs.publicName: Clear a New Mexico record that is not yours
briefs.mechanism: A person wrongfully identified in arrest records or public records as a result of identity theft may petition the district court to expunge those records. On a showing that the person is a victim of identity theft the court shall order expungement and cause the order to be delivered to all relevant law enforcement agencies and courts. The proceeding is a civil petition in district court even where the underlying case was in municipal, magistrate or metropolitan court. Rule 1-077.1 supplies the procedure and its use of Form 4-951 is mandatory; the rule and every form in the set were amended by Supreme Court Order No. S-1-RCR-2024-00099, effective for all cases pending or filed on or after December 31, 2025.

briefs.legalName: Removal of a Record from the Central Repository After a Favourable Disposition (NRS 179A.160)
briefs.publicName: Getting a Nevada arrest off the state repository after a favourable outcome
briefs.mechanism: NRS 179A.160 has now been read in full and it is not a route on which nothing is filed. Subsection 1 provides that where a person has been arrested or issued a citation, or has been the subject of a warrant for alleged criminal conduct, and is acquitted or the disposition of the charge is favourable to the person, then "at any time after the charge is dismissed, acquittal is entered or disposition of the charge in favor of the person is final, the person who is the subject of a record of criminal history relating to the arrest, citation or warrant may apply in writing to the Central Repository and the agency which maintains the record to have it removed from the files which are available and generally searched for the purpose of responding to inquiries concerning the criminal history of a person." Subsection 2 makes removal mandatory — "The Central Repository and the agency shall remove the record unless" one of five stated conditions applies. So the participant makes a written application, to two recipients, with no waiting period and no hearing, and the agencies must act unless an exclusion bites. It remains a repository remedy rather than a court sealing order, so it sits alongside the NRS 179.255 petition rather than replacing it, and subsection 3 preserves a court's separate authority to order deletion or modification of a record. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records, and NRS 179A.160 likewise removes a record from the files that are available and generally searched rather than destroying it. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
briefs.venue: Not a filing route. The court or agency that handled the matter holds the record.

destination.name: The Central Repository for Nevada Records of Criminal History, and the agency which maintains the record
destination.detail: NRS 179A.160(1) directs the application to two recipients and not one: the Central Repository for Nevada Records of Criminal History, administered by the Nevada State Police Records, Communications and Compliance Division at 333 West Nye Lane, Suite 100, Carson City, Nevada 89706, and the agency which maintains the record, ordinarily the arresting agency. The application is made in writing by the person who is the subject of the record. It is not a court filing, no order issues on it, and it does not reach the court's own record, which is why the parallel screen for the court sealing petition matters.

briefs.legalName: Sealing of Records After an Unconditional Pardon (NRS 179.273)
briefs.publicName: Seal a Nevada record after a pardon
briefs.mechanism: NRS 179.273 is titled "Sealing of records after unconditional pardon: Automatic sealing; petition; no fee" in the chapter index published by the Nevada Legislature, and the controlling review describes it as providing automatic sealing together with a no-fee petition route. The internal reference omits the section entirely, which the review records as one of its five substantive gaps. Because sealing is automatic in the first instance, the correct first move is verification rather than a filing; the petition exists for the case where the automatic sealing has not happened, and it carries no fee. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.

briefs.legalName: OSBI Expedited Expungement Request Portal (22 O.S. § 19d, as enacted by Senate Bill 2030, Laws 2026, c. 282)
briefs.publicName: Oklahoma's free expungement request portal, and where it stands
briefs.mechanism: Senate Bill 2030 was enacted and is in force. It was approved by the Governor on 11 May 2026 after the emergency was adopted in both chambers, it is codified as Laws 2026, c. 282, and the codifier records the amendment as effective 1 July 2026. The Act amends 22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19, creates 22 O.S. §§ 18b and 19d, and repeals a duplicate § 18. Sections 19a, 60.18 and 991c are untouched. Section 19d(A) requires the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation to establish and maintain a publicly accessible online portal by 1 November 2026 for individuals to submit an expedited expungement request for clean slate eligible records as defined in § 18b, or records eligible under § 18(A)(16). Section 19d(B) limits what the request may require to sufficient personal identification information for the Bureau to locate the record and contact information for notification. Section 19d(C) sets the review sequence: the Bureau reviews the record, solicits review by the arresting and prosecuting agencies, sends a request to the district court on confirmation, and where any party finds the record ineligible sends the individual a written or electronic notice of rejection stating the reasons. The statute sets no fee for the request. Neither the automatic process nor the portal is operating. The Bureau's own criminal history record expungement page, last updated 23 July 2026 and therefore after the Act took effect, describes no portal and does not state that automatic sealing is operating. Both statutory deadlines are in the future. The right to petition is expressly preserved. Section 19d(G) reads "Nothing in this section precludes an individual from filing a petition with the district court pursuant to Section 19 of Title 22 of the Oklahoma Statutes for expungement of clean slate eligible records", and § 19(A) is undisturbed. The petition routes are the only routes an Oklahoma participant can use today. Records sealed through the clean slate route are PARTIALLY sealed under § 18b(D): unavailable to the public, still available to law enforcement for law enforcement purposes, and still admissible under § 18b(E) to prove a prior conviction or deferred judgment without an unsealing order. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing. Title 22 § 19 does not authorise physical destruction, a sealed record may be unsealed on changed conditions or a compelling reason, and under § 19(L) — the ten-year obliteration rule, which the pre-2026 lettering carried further down the section — a sealed record not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed.
briefs.venue: No venue. The route, when it operates, runs on the State's records rather than on a filing.

destination.name: Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation, with the district court entering the order
destination.detail: Nothing is filed and nothing is generated. When the portal exists the participant submits the request themselves under § 19d(B); the Bureau reviews it, the arresting and prosecuting agencies review it, and the district court enters any order. As things stand the participant is told that the portal is required by statute by 1 November 2026, that it is not published, and is screened for the petition routes in the meantime.

briefs.legalName: Motion to Set Aside the Record of an Arrest, Citation or Charge Where No Accusatory Instrument Was Filed (ORS 137.225(1)(c))
briefs.publicName: Set aside an Oregon arrest that never led to charges
briefs.mechanism: Where no accusatory instrument is filed, at any time after 60 days from the date the prosecuting attorney indicates that the state has elected not to proceed with a prosecution or contempt proceeding, an arrested, cited or charged person may apply to the court in the county in which the person was arrested, cited or charged for an order setting aside the record of the arrest, citation or charge. The clock runs from the prosecutor's declination, not from the arrest. Under ORS 137.225(3)(b) the court shall grant a motion under this paragraph. There is no filing fee under ORS 137.225(1)(g). Oregon calls it a set-aside and there are no separate sealing and expungement tracks: the court sets aside and seals, and under ORS 137.225(4) the conviction, arrest, citation, charge or other proceeding is deemed not to have occurred and the person may answer accordingly any questions relating to its occurrence. The order reaches Oregon court and law enforcement records including the Oregon State Police LEDS system. It does not reach federal or other states' records. Under 2024 Oregon State Police policy a set-aside does not restore firearm rights; a separate restoration process is required. Two statutory carve-outs survive: under ORS 137.225(10) the deemed-not-to-have-occurred rule does not apply in a civil action where truth is an element of a claim or defence, and a party may apply for disclosure; and under ORS 137.225(11) a court may order records reopened on a prosecutor's or defendant's motion supported by affidavit showing good cause, and a prosecuting attorney may unseal a set-aside arrest, citation or charge to initiate a proceeding within the statute of limitations, on written notice to the person.
briefs.venue: The circuit court in the county in which the person was arrested, cited or charged. ORS 137.225(1)(c).

destination.name: Oregon circuit court for the county of arrest, citation or charge
destination.detail: A motion filed with the circuit court, with a copy served on the office of the prosecuting attorney who had authority to prosecute, and a full set of fingerprints forwarded to the Department of State Police. Note ORS 137.225(11)(b): where an arrest, citation or charge set aside under subsection (1)(c) is concerned, a prosecuting attorney may unseal the records to initiate a proceeding within the statute of limitations, on written notice to the person's last known address.

briefs.legalName: Solicitor Application to Destroy Arrest Records After Successful Alcohol Education Program Completion, S.C. Code § 17-22-530(A)
briefs.publicName: Clear a South Carolina underage-alcohol charge after you completed the Alcohol Education Program
briefs.mechanism: The controlling citation is settled at source. Article 5 of Chapter 22, Title 17 is the Alcohol Education Program: § 17-22-510 gives each circuit solicitor prosecutorial discretion to establish the programme, § 17-22-520 sets eligibility, and § 17-22-530 governs disposition on completion. Under § 17-22-530(A), when a person successfully completes an alcohol education programme the circuit solicitor shall effect a noncriminal disposition of the alcohol-related offence and no record may be maintained except by the Commission on Prosecution Coordination to prevent a second use; under § 17-22-530(B) the person may then apply to the court for an order to destroy all official records relating to the arrest. Section 17-22-520 confines eligibility to a person at least seventeen but under twenty-one at the time of arrest, with no prior alcohol-related offence and no significant history of prior delinquency or criminal activity, charged with one of eleven enumerated offences or another offence similar in nature and severity as determined by the circuit solicitor, expressly excluding the offences enumerated in §§ 56-5-2930 and 56-5-2933. Participation is once only. Section 17-22-940(D) names the alcohol education program director as an attestor and § 17-22-940(E)(1) exempts § 17-22-530(A) from the SLED verification fee.
briefs.venue: Statewide statute administered circuit by circuit, each programme being under the direct supervision and control of the circuit solicitor. Apply to the Solicitor's Office in the judicial circuit where the offence was committed.

destination.name: Solicitor's Office in the judicial circuit where the offence was committed
destination.detail: The applicant applies to the solicitor's office. The alcohol education program director must attest by signature under § 17-22-940(D) before the solicitor and then a circuit court judge sign. No SLED verification fee is charged.

briefs.legalName: Solicitor Application to Expunge Records After a First-Offence Drug Conditional Discharge, S.C. Code § 44-53-450(b)
briefs.publicName: Clear a first South Carolina drug possession case that ended in a conditional discharge
briefs.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 44-53-450(A) allows a person not previously convicted of any offence under Article 3 of Chapter 53, Title 44, or under any state or federal marijuana, stimulant, depressant or hallucinogenic drug statute, who pleads guilty to or is found guilty of possession of a controlled substance under § 44-53-370(c) or (d) or § 44-53-375(A), to be placed on probation without entry of a judgment of guilt, with the court discharging the person and dismissing the proceedings on fulfilment of the terms. The discharge is not a conviction for purposes of any disqualification or disability, a nonpublic record is retained by the Department of Narcotic and Dangerous Drugs under SLED solely to determine whether a later offence is a subsequent one, and the discharge and dismissal may occur only once with respect to any person. Subsection (B) is the expungement: on dismissal and discharge the person may apply to the court for an order expunging from all official records, other than the retained nonpublic record, all recordation relating to the arrest, indictment or information, trial, finding of guilt, and the dismissal and discharge, and if the court determines after hearing that the person was dismissed and discharged it shall enter the order, restoring the person in the contemplation of law to the status occupied before arrest. Subsection (C) requires payment before discharge of a fee of $350 in general sessions court or $150 in summary court, waivable, reducible or suspendable only for indigency. Section 17-22-940(D) requires the summary court judge to attest where the matter was in summary court, and § 17-22-940(E) exempts the route from SLED verification and its fee.
briefs.venue: Statewide statute. The conditional discharge itself may be entered in general sessions or summary court; the expungement application runs through the Solicitor's Office in the circuit where the offence was committed.

briefs.legalName: Solicitor Application to Destroy Arrest Records After Successful Traffic Education Program Completion, S.C. Code § 17-22-330(A)
briefs.publicName: Clear a South Carolina traffic charge after you completed the Traffic Education Program
briefs.mechanism: The controlling citation is settled at source. Article 3 of Chapter 22, Title 17 is the Traffic Education Program Act: § 17-22-310 gives each circuit solicitor prosecutorial discretion to establish a programme for persons who commit traffic-related offences punishable only by a fine and loss of four points or less, and bars participation where the offence resulted in death or serious bodily injury; § 17-22-320 confines eligibility to a person with no significant history of traffic violations and allows participation only once; and § 17-22-330(A) provides that on successful completion the administering governmental agency shall effect a noncriminal disposition of the offence, with no record maintained except by the programme to prevent a second use. Subsections (C) and (D) allow termination and reinstatement for violating the conditions, and require termination where the person receives a subsequent traffic violation in the six months following the ticket. Section 17-22-940(D) names the traffic education program director as an attestor and § 17-22-940(E)(1) exempts § 17-22-330(A) from the SLED verification fee.

briefs.legalName: Expunction after trial court acquittal, Tex. Code Crim. Proc. arts. 55A.002 and 55A.201
briefs.publicName: Clear a record after being found not guilty
briefs.mechanism: A person tried and acquitted by the trial court is entitled to expunction. Under art. 55A.201 the order shall be entered not later than the 30th day after the date of acquittal, on request of the acquitted person after notice to the state, or on request of the attorney representing the state with the person's consent. On acquittal the trial court shall advise the person of the right to expunction. The requesting party must provide the information required in an art. 55A.253 petition. The order is prepared by the acquitted person's attorney if the person was represented, otherwise by the attorney representing the state. Where the 30-day window has closed or the court did not act, the person falls back to an ordinary ex parte petition under art. 55A.251, which lists art. 55A.002 among the qualifying entitlements. Article 55A.151 bars relief where the acquitted offence arose out of a criminal episode as defined by Penal Code 3.01 and the person was convicted of, or remains subject to prosecution for, at least one other offence in that episode. Under art. 102.0061(c), read at source on 2026-08-06, the filing fee must be waived where the expunction relates to an acquittal other than one described by art. 55A.151 and the petition is filed not later than the 30th day after the acquittal.
briefs.venue: In-window: the trial court if it is a district, justice or municipal court of record, or a district court in the county where the trial court sits (art. 55A.201(a)). Out-of-window: a district court for the county of arrest or of the alleged offence under art. 55A.251, or a justice or municipal court of record under art. 55A.252 for a fine-only arrest. Statewide across all 254 counties.

destination.name: The trial court within the window, otherwise a district court for the county of arrest or of the alleged offence
destination.detail: No statewide expunction form exists at any level of Texas state government, so there is no statewide form to be rejected locally. What varies by county is formatting practice: civil cover sheets, sensitive-data handling, hearing-setting procedure, copy counts, and whether the clerk or the filer prepares the notice of hearing. Article 55A.253(c) requires each district clerk to publish the agency and e-mail list on the clerk's website, so that list is itself county-specific and is the first place the packet sends the participant.

briefs.legalName: Order of nondisclosure after community supervision following a misdemeanour conviction, Tex. Gov't Code 411.073
briefs.publicName: Seal a misdemeanour conviction after successfully completing probation

The waiting period is immediate on completion of community supervision, except that a misdemeanour under Penal Code Chapters 20, 21, 22, 25, 42, 43 or 46 waits until the second anniversary of completion. This is the ordinary route for a probated misdemeanour conviction and is probably the highest-volume conviction track in the state. Section 411.073 was last amended in 2017 and was not touched in 2025 or 2026.

briefs.legalName: Order of nondisclosure after successful completion of a veterans treatment court programme, Tex. Gov't Code 411.0727
briefs.publicName: Seal a record after completing veterans treatment court
briefs.mechanism: Successful completion of a veterans treatment court programme as defined by Government Code Chapter 124 or former law. The waiting period is the second anniversary of the date of successful completion, and a felony conviction at any time during those two years defeats it. Under 411.0727(e) the section is not available where entry into the programme arose from an offence involving operating a motor vehicle while intoxicated. A prior conviction for any offence on the section's own exclusion list also defeats it. Section 411.0727 was last amended in 2017 and was not touched in 2025 or 2026. The overlap with expunction is decisive and is routing logic rather than an optimisation: a veterans treatment court dismissal may also support expunction under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 55A.053(a)(2)(A) with the streamlined 30-day order under art. 55A.203 and no fee, and expunction is the stronger remedy because it destroys rather than seals.
briefs.venue: Statewide in scope with court-level filing. briefs.legalName: Motion to remove the link between personal identifying information and a dismissed criminal case, Utah Code 77-40a-105
briefs.publicName: Break the link between your name and a dismissed case
briefs.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06. An individual whose criminal case is dismissed may move the court for an order removing the link between the individual's personal identifying information and the dismissed case in any publicly searchable database of the Utah state courts. Personal identifying information means a current name, former name, nickname or alias, together with date of birth. The court shall grant the motion if 30 days have passed from the day the case was dismissed, no appeal was filed within that 30-day period, and no charge in the case was a domestic violence offence as defined in Section 77-36-1. Relief is ministerial rather than discretionary once those three conditions are met. Two express limits define what the remedy is worth: under subsection (3) removing the link does not affect a prosecuting, arresting or other agency's records, and under subsection (4) the case history, unless expunged under the chapter, remains public and accessible through a search by case number. The remedy therefore breaks the name-to-case search path in the state courts' public database and does nothing else. The companion provision at Utah Code 78B-7-1002.1 gives the same relief to a person against whom a civil protective order or civil stalking injunction was sought and denied; that branch is a civil matter outside the record-clearing product scope and is not built here.
briefs.venue: The court that handled the dismissed criminal case. Form 1501CR carries a district-or-justice-court election on its face, so the remedy runs in both court levels. Whether a judge or a court commissioner decides turns on the case category and the judicial district, which is why Utah Courts publishes a judge version and a commissioner version of the same motion.

destination.name: The district or justice court that dismissed the criminal case
destination.detail: The participant files the motion in the court that handled the case, on the existing case rather than as a new action, and the court enters the order on form 1502CR. The order reaches only the Utah state courts' publicly searchable database; prosecuting, arresting and other agency records are untouched, and the case history remains findable by case number.

briefs.legalName: Petition for Expungement Where Another Person Used the Petitioner's Identity, Va. Code § 19.2-392.2(B)
briefs.publicName: Clear a Virginia record created when someone else used your name
briefs.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06, the exact subsection is § 19.2-392.2(B): if any person whose name or other identification has been used without his consent or authorisation by another person who has been charged or arrested using such name or identification, he may file a petition with the court disposing of the charge for relief under the section, without paying any court fees or costs, and the petition shall include one complete set of the petitioner's fingerprints obtained from a law-enforcement agency. Subsection E prescribes the proof route the controlling review could not verify: the petitioner obtains the fingerprint set from a law-enforcement agency and gives that agency a copy of the petition; the agency submits the fingerprints to the CCRE with the petition attached; the CCRE forwards the criminal history and the fingerprint set to the court under seal; on completion of the hearing the court returns the fingerprint card, and where no hearing was held the card is destroyed unless the petitioner asks for it back within thirty days or supplies a stamped self-addressed envelope. Subsection H supplies a distinct and faster route where the charge is dismissed because the court finds the person arrested or charged is not the person named in the summons, warrant, indictment or presentment: the dismissing court, on motion of the person improperly charged, enters the expungement order.
briefs.venue: The court disposing of the charge, per § 19.2-392.2(B). Where the misidentification route in subsection (H) applies, the order is entered by the court dismissing the charge.

briefs.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Police and Court Records of a Non-Conviction, Va. Code § 19.2-392.2(A)
briefs.publicName: Expunge a Virginia charge that did not end in a conviction
briefs.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06 in the version effective until December 1, 2026, § 19.2-392.2(A) allows a person charged with a crime, a civil offence or any offence defined in Title 18.2 who is acquitted, or against whom a nolle prosequi is taken or the charge is otherwise dismissed including dismissal by accord and satisfaction under § 19.2-151, to petition for expungement of the police and court records relating to the charge, and provides that no court fees or costs are payable. Subsection C fixes venue in the circuit court of the county or city where the case was disposed of, prescribes the petition contents, and requires the petitioner to request that the CCRE electronically forward a copy of the petitioner's Virginia criminal history record to that court. Subsection D gives the attorney for the Commonwealth twenty-one days to object, answer or give written notice of no objection. Subsection F applies the manifest injustice standard but adds a presumption the controlling review could not verify: where the petitioner has no prior criminal record and the arrest was for a misdemeanor violation or the charge was a civil offence, the petitioner is entitled to expungement in the absence of good cause shown to the contrary by the Commonwealth. Subsection F also allows the court to enter the order without a hearing where the Commonwealth gives written notice of no objection and, for a felony charge, stipulates manifest injustice. Subsection K makes State Police validate the accuracy of the record but not its eligibility. Subsection L makes an order voidable within three years. Subsection M keeps the petition and any responsive pleadings under seal.

briefs.legalName: Petition to Seal an Enumerated Offence After Seven Clean Years, Va. Code § 19.2-392.12:1(A)
briefs.publicName: Seal an eligible minor Virginia conviction after seven clean years
briefs.mechanism: A free-standing petition track, not a backstop. Section 19.2-392.12:1(A) reaches an exhaustive list of offence provisions — a violation of § 4.1-305; a misdemeanor violation of § 18.2-96 or § 18.2-103; a violation of § 18.2-119, § 18.2-120 or § 18.2-134; a misdemeanor violation of § 18.2-248.1; a violation of subsection A of § 18.2-265.3; or a violation of § 18.2-415 — whether the disposition was a conviction or a deferred and dismissed charge, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. The single test is seven years since the date of conviction or of dismissal of the deferred charge with no conviction in that period of any law requiring a report to the CCRE under § 19.2-390(A), or of any other state, the District of Columbia, the United States or any territory, excluding Title 46.2 traffic infractions. What is not required is the whole of what makes § 19.2-392.12 hard: no manifest injustice, no rehabilitation showing, no restitution criterion, no felony-history bars, and no lifetime cap, subsection E confirming both that there is no limit on the number of petitions and that grants here do not count against the two-petition cap in § 19.2-392.12. Subsection I makes the outcome mandatory on the two findings. Subsection D carries a same-date rule: the petition may not seek sealing where the charge, conviction or ancillary matter was finalised on the same date as a conviction or deferred dismissal that is not eligible under the section. One petition may cover multiple charges, convictions and ancillary matters provided all are eligible.

briefs.legalName: Petition to Seal a Class 5 or 6 Felony or an 18.2-95 Larceny Felony, Va. Code § 19.2-392.12
briefs.publicName: Seal an eligible Virginia felony conviction after ten clean years
briefs.mechanism: Petition sealing under § 19.2-392.12 reaching a conviction of, or a deferred and dismissed charge for, a Class 5 or 6 felony, or a violation of § 18.2-95 or any other felony offence in which the defendant is deemed guilty of larceny and punished as provided in § 18.2-95, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. Ten years must have passed with no reportable conviction, and the clock runs from the latest of five events, not two: dismissal of the deferred charge, conviction, release from incarceration, a finding that the person violated a suspended sentence, probation or parole, or release from incarceration following such a finding. A probation violation therefore restarts the clock. Three felony-history bars apply: never convicted of a Class 1 or 2 felony or any other felony punishable by life; no Class 3 or 4 felony conviction within the past twenty years; and no other felony conviction within the past ten years from the date the petition was filed. Four further criteria the internal reference omits entirely: rehabilitation demonstrated where the records indicate the occurrence involved the use of or dependence upon alcohol, a narcotic drug or any other self-administered intoxicant; court-ordered restitution on any charge, conviction or ancillary matter in the petition paid in full; not previously having obtained sealing of two other deferrals or convictions arising out of different sentencing events; and manifest injustice, which is a statutory condition of sealing and not merely of expungement. Subsection C caps the section at two petitions granted in a lifetime and confines one petition to charges arising out of the same transaction or occurrence, ancillary matters not counting as separate transactions. Subsection L carries a nineteen-subdivision exclusion list of enumerated Code sections. There is no fee, the Commonwealth has thirty days, a written notice of no objection stipulating eligibility and manifest injustice permits an order without a hearing, and subsection J makes an order voidable on motion within two years.

briefs.legalName: Petition to Seal a Misdemeanour Conviction or Deferred Dismissal, Va. Code § 19.2-392.12
briefs.publicName: Seal a Virginia misdemeanour conviction after seven clean years
briefs.mechanism: Petition sealing under § 19.2-392.12 reaching a conviction of, or a charge deferred and dismissed for, a misdemeanor, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. Seven years must have passed with no reportable conviction, and the clock runs from the latest of five events, not two: dismissal of the deferred charge, conviction, release from incarceration, a finding that the person violated a suspended sentence, probation or parole, or release from incarceration following such a finding. A probation violation therefore restarts the clock. Three felony-history bars apply: never convicted of a Class 1 or 2 felony or any other felony punishable by life; no Class 3 or 4 felony conviction within the past twenty years; and no other felony conviction within the past ten years from the date the petition was filed. Four further criteria the internal reference omits entirely: rehabilitation demonstrated where the records indicate the occurrence involved the use of or dependence upon alcohol, a narcotic drug or any other self-administered intoxicant; court-ordered restitution on any charge, conviction or ancillary matter in the petition paid in full; not previously having obtained sealing of two other deferrals or convictions arising out of different sentencing events; and manifest injustice, which is a statutory condition of sealing and not merely of expungement. Subsection C caps the section at two petitions granted in a lifetime and confines one petition to charges arising out of the same transaction or occurrence, ancillary matters not counting as separate transactions. Subsection L carries a nineteen-subdivision exclusion list of enumerated Code sections. There is no fee, the Commonwealth has thirty days, a written notice of no objection stipulating eligibility and manifest injustice permits an order without a hearing, and subsection J makes an order voidable on motion within two years.

briefs.legalName: Expungement on discharge from a deferred sentence, 13 V.S.A. § 7041(e)
briefs.publicName: Records cleared after completing a deferred sentence
briefs.mechanism: On fulfilment of the terms of probation and of the deferred sentence agreement, the court shall strike the adjudication of guilt and discharge the person. Except as provided in subsection (h), the record of the criminal proceedings shall be expunged on discharge from probation, absent a finding of good cause by the court, and the court shall issue an order to expunge all records and files related to the arrest, citation, investigation, charge, adjudication of guilt, criminal proceedings and probation. Copies go to each agency, department or official named, and thereafter the court, law enforcement officers, agencies and departments reply that no record exists. Notwithstanding the subsection, the record is not expunged until restitution has been paid in full. Read at source on 2026-08-06: § 7041 sits in chapter 221, was not amended by Act 60, and its relief is court-driven — no petition is required and the participant files nothing to obtain it. Subsection (h) requires VCIC to retain a confidential special index of deferred sentences for sex offences requiring registration, accessible only by the VCIC director and one designated staff person for presentence investigation purposes.

destination.detail: On the ordinary path the court acts on its own on discharge and the participant submits nothing. Where the order did not issue, the written request goes back to the same court. The court sends copies of the order to each agency, department or official named in it.

briefs.legalName: Sealing after an unconditional pardon, 13 V.S.A. § 7601(4)(B)(iv) and § 7602(d)
briefs.publicName: Seal a record after a Governor's pardon
briefs.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06. Section 7601(4)(B)(iv) makes any offence for which the person has been granted an unconditional pardon from the Governor a qualifying felony. The pardon therefore changes the offence's status rather than its disposition, and it leads to sealing rather than expungement. Because the pardon route sits in the qualifying-felony subsection, the seven-year clock at § 7602(d) appears to apply even to a pardoned misdemeanour; whether a pardoned misdemeanour instead runs on the three-year clock at § 7602(c) is not resolved by the text. A pardon is not itself record relief in Vermont: it makes the offence a qualifying crime for sealing, and the sealing petition is still required.
briefs.venue: The Criminal Division of the Vermont Superior Court (13 V.S.A. § 7601(1)), in the county that handled the case. Vermont has a unified Superior Court and one statewide Judiciary form set, with no county form variation identified.

destination.name: Criminal Division of the Vermont Superior Court, in the county that handled the case
destination.detail: Whichever office prosecuted the offence, the State's Attorney or the Attorney General, unless that office authorises the other to act (§ 7602(a)(3)).

legalDesignLimitations.statement: After 2025-07-01 Vermont is a sealing state, not an expungement state. Participant-facing copy must not use expungement as the umbrella term: expungement removes records from any accessible database and destroys the paper file, sealing moves them into a confidential file without destroying them, and after Act 60 expungement survives only for conduct that is no longer criminal.

On the § 7602 conviction tracks and on § 7609 the statute is drafted against the State: the court shall grant if the respondent has failed to show that sealing would be contrary to the interests of justice. This is not a petitioner-side public-interest burden and the packet must not write it as one.

The stipulation is a request, not an entitlement, and the prosecutor's refusal converts a paper decision into a hearing the participant must attend. A Vermont packet must say that plainly before the participant pays, and it must not describe a stipulation as though signature were a formality.
CDL bar reaches all motor vehicle offenses, not just DUI.
Restitution condition reaches any conviction, not just the target offense.
Separate petition per offense where offenses are unrelated or in different counties.
Pending charge anywhere freezes the petition.
Denial carries a 2-year refiling bar.

Expunged and sealed records may still appear in a federal criminal background check. Vermont relief does not reach federal records even though VCIC notifies the FBI's National Crime Information Center.

At least four versions of the 200-00130A instruction guide have been live on vtcourts.gov, including 07/2017, 01/2018 and 02/2020 revisions that predate Act 60 and describe expungement categories that no longer exist. Only the version linked from the live expungement page may be used, and any archived copy in the LegalEase library is superseded until its revision date is checked against the live link.
A pardon is not itself record relief in Vermont. It makes the offence a qualifying crime for sealing, and the sealing petition is still required.

briefs.legalName: Application for a Certificate of Restoration of Opportunity, RCW 9.97.020
briefs.publicName: Get a Washington court certificate that stops most licensing bodies disqualifying you for your record
briefs.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06. A certificate of restoration of opportunity is a court-issued instrument that operates on the collateral consequences of a conviction rather than on the record itself, and RCW 9.94A.030(11) treats issued certificates as part of the criminal history a sentencing court sees, which confirms it is a recognised instrument rather than an informal document. Its operative effect is at RCW 9.97.020(1): no state, county or municipal department, board, officer or agency authorised to assess the qualifications of an applicant for a licence, certificate of authority, qualification to engage in a profession or business, or admission to a qualifying examination may disqualify a qualified applicant solely on the basis of criminal history where the applicant holds a certificate and meets all other statutory and regulatory requirements, except as required by federal law or as exempted. The exemptions are extensive and must be encoded: criminal justice agencies as defined in RCW 10.97.030 and the Washington State Bar Association are exempt outright, and the section does not apply to the licensing, certification or qualification of accountants, bail bond agents, escrow agents, nursing home administrators, nursing, physicians and physician assistants, private investigators, receivers, teachers, notaries public, real estate brokers and salespersons, security guards, and vulnerable adult care providers who are not home care aides or contracted providers or licensees as defined in RCW 43.20A.715. The Department of Social and Health Services and its contracted providers and licensees retain sole discretion whether to consider a certificate when hiring or licensing for positions caring for or having unsupervised access to vulnerable adults or children. Nothing in the section restores or creates a means to restore firearm rights or eligibility for a firearm dealer licence under RCW 9.41.110, and nothing requires the removal of a protection order. Eligibility is set by the RCW 9.97.010(1) definition of qualified applicant, on a graduated scale: one year from sentencing for a misdemeanour or gross misdemeanour probation, deferred or other noncustodial sentence; eighteen months from release from confinement on such an offence; two years from sentencing, or from release from confinement, for a class B or C felony; and five years from sentencing, or from release, for a violent offence as defined in RCW 9.94A.030. The applicant must also be in compliance with or have completed all sentencing requirements, including having paid legal financial obligations in full, being fully compliant with a payment plan, or being out of compliance with a payment plan but having established good cause with the court. And the applicant must never have been convicted of a class A felony or an attempt, solicitation or conspiracy to commit one, a sex offence as defined in RCW 9.94A.030, a crime including sexual motivation under RCW 9.94A.835, RCW 13.40.135 or RCW 9.94A.535(3)(f), or extortion in the first degree, among the further bars in that subsection. The procedural half of the section was read at source on 2026-08-08 and is carried here. RCW 9.97.010(2) defines a qualified court as any Washington superior court in the county where the applicant resides or that sentenced or adjudicated them, and provides that where the sentencing or adjudicating court was a court of limited jurisdiction the qualified court is the superior court in the county of conviction or adjudication; a district or municipal court is therefore never itself a qualified court. RCW 9.97.020(2) gives a qualified court jurisdiction to issue a certificate to a qualified applicant, and RCW 9.97.020(2)(a) leaves it to that court's discretion whether the certificate applies to all past criminal history or only to the convictions or adjudications in the jurisdiction of the court. The application is filed as a civil action under RCW 9.97.020(7). Under RCW 9.97.020(6) the applicant must notify the prosecutor in the county where the certificate is sought, and must also notify the prosecuting attorney in any other jurisdiction that sentenced the applicant in the five years preceding the application; the prosecutor in the county of application supplies the court with a report of the applicant's criminal history. Under RCW 9.97.020(8) a superior court in the county in which the applicant resides may decline to consider the application, in which case it must dismiss without prejudice, state the reason on the order, and the applicant may refile in another qualified court, while the superior court in the county of the applicant's conviction or adjudication may not decline to consider the application; a court of either county that finds the applicant not qualified must likewise dismiss without prejudice and state the reasons on the order. The section provides no transfer procedure: the remedy for a declining court is dismissal and refiling by the applicant, not transfer by the court. Under RCW 9.97.020(9) the court decides without a hearing on the application and the prosecutor's pleadings unless it determines a hearing is necessary, and under RCW 9.97.020(10) the clerk of the granting court transmits the certificate to the Washington State Patrol identification section. RCW 9.97.020(11) directs the Administrative Office of the Courts to develop instructions, forms and an informational brochure, including at least a sample standard application and a form order, distributed to all county clerks and superior courts and translated into the state's significant non-English-speaking languages.
briefs.venue: A qualified court, and RCW 9.97.010(2) closes the set: a Washington superior court in the county where the applicant resides, or the superior court of the county that sentenced or adjudicated them. Where the sentencing or adjudicating court was a court of limited jurisdiction, the qualified court is the superior court of that county of conviction or adjudication; the district or municipal court that convicted the applicant is never itself a qualified court. Because the set is closed and statutory, one statewide packet serves the whole state as to venue and the county is a participant answer rather than a routing branch. The packet routes to the superior court of the county of the applicant's conviction or adjudication, because RCW 9.97.020(8) provides that court may not decline to consider the application.

destination.name: The superior court of a qualified county under RCW 9.97.010(2)
destination.detail: Filed as a civil action under RCW 9.97.020(7), at the superior court clerk's office of the chosen qualified county, with the notice to each prosecuting attorney RCW 9.97.020(6) requires. The packet routes to the superior court of the county of conviction or adjudication because RCW 9.97.020(8) provides that it may not decline to consider the application. The superior court of the county where the applicant resides remains statutorily available and may be nearer, and a participant who prefers it may use it, but that court may decline to consider the application; if it does, it must dismiss without prejudice, must state the reason on the order, and the applicant may refile in another qualified court. There is no statutory transfer procedure: the remedy is refiling by the applicant, not transfer by the court. Confirming intake with the clerk is prudent practice and not a legal prerequisite, and it is not a condition of generating this packet; which counties require additional accompanying documents under local superior court rules is a separate open filing-instruction question.
